misconceptions.description: Treating a storyboard frame as a picture of the screen rather than as a testable claim about what the learner will do and learn
misconceptions.trigger: frame caption describes appearance (colors, layout) but states no learning claim or learner action
misconceptions.feedback: Rewrite the frame caption as a claim: who does what, and what evidence on the next frame would show the claim held. A frame is an argument, not a snapshot.

misconceptions.description: Stating a frame-level claim with no warrant from Mayer or cognitive load theory that would justify why the frame should produce the claimed learning
misconceptions.trigger: learner asserts a frame helps learning but cites no principle and no expected processing change
misconceptions.feedback: Attach one warrant. Name the principle (for example, signaling or coherence) and state the processing it is meant to change on this frame.

misconceptions.description: Writing a frame claim so vague that no prototype observation could ever contradict it
misconceptions.trigger: claim uses words like clearer or engaging with no observable learner behavior attached
misconceptions.feedback: State what an observer would see if the frame failed. If nothing could disconfirm the claim, it is decoration, not a design decision.

misconceptions.description: Judging a single frame as if it stood alone, ignoring how the prior frame set up the claim and the next frame tests it
misconceptions.trigger: learner revises one frame without checking the claim it inherits or hands off
misconceptions.feedback: Trace the claim across three frames: setup, claim, evidence. A frame that breaks the chain weakens the whole storyboard argument.
